title: I Asked One Question. My Students Had a Lot to Say.
author: Jennifer Haber
summary: Jennifer Haber, a middle school English teacher, describes the second-day activity she calls the Take Care of Me List, built around one question: what do I need to know to take care of you this year? Each student privately writes five to seven things they want their teacher to know as a learner and as a person. This year she read nearly six hundred answers from ninety students and groups them by theme, quoting the students' own words. Students ask not to be misread as disrespectful, to be allowed to move, to be called on or left alone depending on temperament, to receive honest feedback, to have their questions answered patiently, and to be understood in the struggles with reading, writing and life outside school that teachers cannot see. Haber argues that many students describe past teachers who misjudged them because nobody asked, and that a single question can surface in a day what might otherwise take weeks to learn.
points: A single open question, what do I need to know to take care of you, produces more honest information about students in one day than weeks of icebreakers.
Because the lists are private, students disclose things they would never say aloud, such as anxiety about presenting, family upheaval and difficult schedules.
The same teaching move can help one student and hurt another, for example cold calling or reading aloud, so individual knowledge of students matters more than a uniform policy.
Behaviour such as fidgeting, doodling, talking or side-eyeing is often misread, and knowing the reason lets a teacher respond with patience instead of correction.
Students want specific, honest feedback and straight talk about difficulty, and their repeated questions can signal that directions were less clear than the teacher thought.
quotes: So instead of coming up with some complicated game or icebreaker, I decided to ask just one question: What do I need to know to take care of you this year?
This year I read close to six hundred answers from ninety students, and they were some of the most honest lists I’ve ever received.
What I keep thinking about is how easy it would be to misread these students. I might see someone talking or looking annoyed and assume they don’t care, when that may not be true at all.
If I hadn’t asked, I would have had no way to know that the same teaching strategy could help one student and make another miserable.
I read, “I asked what I could do better and they said that I know. I don’t know,” twice because it says the whole thing better than I could.

When a student asks a lot of questions, I want to remember that they may just be trying very hard to understand. I also need to notice when all those questions might be telling me that my directions weren’t nearly as clear as I thought they were.
As I read these lists, I kept noticing how many students described being misunderstood by a teacher in the past.
We spend all day asking students questions about what we’re teaching them, but not nearly enough about what school feels like for them.
